 Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” impacts how students receive FAFSA
 In POLITICS 
 Nov 17, 2026
 By James Swilling 
 Photography by Stephen Day 
 107 Views
 0 Comments 
 Pedestrians cross CSUSB’s San Bernardino campus with the foothills in view. 
 Stephen Day 
 With drastic changes to FAFSA, going to college is becoming a very different task than it used to be.
 On July 4, 2025, Donald Trump and the House of Representatives passed the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” or OBBBA. The bill overhauled part of the country’s budget, cutting over one trillion dollars in funding for healthcare and nutrition assistance in education. It also made several changes to FAFSA, loans, and how people receive them, and eliminated unemployment deferment programs.
 Graduate students can no longer use “Grad PLUS Loans” after reaching the standard federal loan limit. Grants for graduate students are now typically limited to $20,000 per year and $100,000 total, while certain programs like law and medicine have a higher limit of $50,000 per year and $200,000 total.
 The bill also changed how students can pay off their loans. Students who take out loans have fewer repayment options, which doesn’t help when unemployment and deferment programs were completely ended, making it harder to pay them back.
 All of these things can impact students not only at CSUSB but all around America. The OBBBA made certain healthcare plans more expensive, eliminated unemployment aid, and, worst of all, made drastic cuts and changes to FAFSA that started the summer before the 2026-2027 school year.
 All of these negatives were disguised as something beneficial because of the overall tax cut that came with the OBBBA.
 For anyone who filled out the FAFSA form before the 2026-2027 school year, their grants will not change as long as they are enrolled.
 Families who have multiple kids in school may have seen their FAFSA forms this summer, despite having the same income information for both students, and seen the younger, first-year college student get a significantly smaller loan from FAFSA.
 FAFSA has also undergone changes that the bill didn’t directly cause. Instead of dividing the expected grant total between the recipients, FAFSA now calculates each student’s eligibility separately. This means two students from the same family, with the same information, can receive different financial aid offers.
 Because FAFSA has changed so much, students at CSUSB and around the country now have to navigate a drastically different financial aid situation. With changes to federal loan limits, repayment options, and the lack of unemployment programs, college could look much more financially daunting. Students and families should be prepared for these changes and expect school to be relatively more expensive.
 James Swilling 
 Practicum Student
